title: The mobile visit for a logistics company
excerpt: An operator will judge the carrier on a phone, often in a yard. The first screen has to show the move and a way to request a quote. Design that screen before the desktop layout.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it, a desk checking the page the way a phone visit should be checked.
caption: A silver laptop on a white desk, with a monitor, a mug, and a phone. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What has to fit on the first phone screen?
faqs.answer: The move, in words an operator uses, and one control to request a quote. Tracking and careers can live in the menu. If the visitor must scroll past a port photograph to learn the mode, the desktop layout has been allowed to decide the phone page.

faqs.question: Which speed targets matter on that screen?
faqs.answer: web.dev's good thresholds are a useful brief: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, and cumulative layout shift under 0.1. The quote button should not jump when the picture arrives, and the words of the move should be in the page, not only inside the image.

faqs.question: Should the mobile menu use shorter labels?
faqs.answer: Use the same job labels as the rest of the site, including the same words for the quote. A vaguer mobile menu creates a second map. Keep Quote and Track visually distinct so a thumb in bright light does not open the wrong one.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The logistics company mobile website is where an operator will judge you. They are often in a yard, on a dock, or between two calls, and the first screen still has to show the work, not a globe, and a way to request a quote. Do not let the desktop composition decide that screen.

Design the phone page as the page. The wide layout is a later adaptation.

## The first screen in a yard

Look at what fits before any scroll, with the browser chrome taking its share. You need the move, in words, and a picture that still contains the freight after the crop. You need one control that says request a quote. The company name can be small. A sentence about global reach cannot be the thing that fits.

If the hero becomes sky and a corner of a container once it is cropped, the frame is wrong for this visit. Put the facts in the first lines of type. "Dry van. Dock to dock. Quote before 2pm." Three lines can carry the offer while the picture loads, and they remain if the picture fails.

Nielsen Norman Group's finding still applies with a thumb. People often leave in 10 to 20 seconds, and the value has to be clear within about 10. Those seconds include the time the page takes to become stable. A hero that jumps when the font arrives, or a banner that pushes the quote below the fold, spends the visit before the move is readable.

Put the quote control where a thumb reaches it without covering the freight. A bar pinned to the bottom can work if it does not hide the one fact they needed, such as the cutoff or the refusal. A button that only exists in a desktop hero, and on the phone sits under a paragraph and a logo row, is a button for people who already decided to hire you.

## What the wide layout breaks

A two-column hero that puts type on the left and a port on the right will stack in an order the framework chose. Choose the stack. The move, then the quote. Do not let a desktop frame in Figma decide the DOM, or the phone will lead with the picture you already know is weak.

Equal buttons get worse when they stack. "Quote" and "Track" and "Careers" as three filled buttons occupy the whole decision and still refuse to say what the first screen is for. Keep one primary control. Tracking belongs in the menu for someone who has a number. Careers belong in the footer. The first screen is for the load that has not been tendered.

Hover tips that explain detention, tiny footnotes, and a rate that only appears on a wide monitor do not exist in the yard. If the shape of the price matters, it is text on the first or second screen. "Dock to dock. Liftgate is extra." One or two lines. A dotted underline is a secret.

Background video of a coastline, a carousel of modes, and an entrance animation are how a desktop comp tries to feel expensive. On a phone they delay the move and move the button. Ship the still. If motion remains, keep it short, and honor a reduced-motion setting rather than making motion the only way to understand the page.

## Speed is part of the quote

web.dev defines the current good thresholds for the three Core Web Vitals: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, and cumulative layout shift under 0.1. Those numbers are a practical brief. The first screen is the largest thing in view. The quote control is the interaction. A layout that shifts will make someone tap Track when they meant Quote.

Treat the hero as a budget. Deliver a photograph sized for the phone, not a desktop original the browser shrinks. Keep the words of the move in HTML so they appear before the image and survive if the image fails. Text baked into the picture cannot be updated when a cutoff changes, and it disappears for anyone who does not see the picture.

A late chat widget, a cookie wall over the button, and a promotional banner that arrives after first paint are layout shift and a wrong tap together. If you need a consent notice, keep it out of the quote path. If you need chat, do not let it be the first thing a coordinator hits when they are trying to price a load.

Test on a mid-range phone on a connection that resembles a warehouse, not only on the office wifi. The page can feel instant in a local preview and still miss the opening where the freight actually is. Fix the opening before you add a section lower down.

## The second screen

After the move and the quote, answer the objection that stops a tender. Usually that is "what do you need from me, and what will you refuse?" Origin, destination, ready date, weight, and a description. The states or the equipment. One refusal in plain words. Then a repeated quote control.

Do not spend the second screen on a mission about the future of freight. They already gave you the first screen. A boundary they can read with one thumb is a reason to continue. A manifesto is a reason to go back to the other tab, where another carrier published a cutoff.

If the quote form starts here, ask for the facts they know, not a survey. Five fields can price a standard move. A ten-field form that asks for company size, a timeline, a budget range, and "how did you hear about us" is a marketing form parked on a dock. Save the extras for after you have replied with a rate or a no.

The menu uses the same job labels as the rest of the site. Do not invent a shorter set for mobile that says "Explore." Quote, rates, track, and one real move should be the list they see.

## Review it outside

Hold the phone at arm's length in bright light, because that is the light on a yard. Gray type on a photograph of a sky will disappear. The move and the button need contrast that survives glare. Then hand the phone to someone who has booked freight. Ask what you move and what they would tap. If they say "logistics" and cannot name a mode, the desktop picture won.

Watch for mis-taps. Quote and Track placed too close, in similar colors, will be hit wrong. Give the quote control space. Make Track a text item in the menu until someone has a number, or style it so it cannot be confused with the commercial door.

Check the largest system text size. If the quote label truncates or the move wraps over the button, the layout is unfinished. A layout that only works at the default size works for the team that designed it.

Do one pass with the address bar expanded and the gesture area reserved. If the pinned button sits under the system gesture, move it. The browser is part of the layout. A frame in a design tool that ignores it will look finished and fail in the hand.

## Build from the phone width

Start the design frame at a phone width. Write the first screen there. Only then ask how the blocks sit on a wide monitor. A wide screen can add margin and a larger crop of the same evidence. It should not add a different argument, a second headline, or the container you rejected.

Review on a device, on the production URL. A preview on a laptop cannot tell you whether the button jumps when the type loads or whether the image delays the move. File those bugs against the first screen before you debate the footer.

Keep one quote URL. The first screen, the header, and the campaign all hit the same short path, with the same fields. A mobile-only form that asks different questions will fill the desk with two kinds of notes and no shared idea of a complete quote.

## A release list for the yard

Check the production URL on a phone, outdoors if you can. Match visible without scroll. One quote label. The next screen states a refusal or a cutoff. Track is not an equal button. The picture does not shove the control after it loads. The largest text size still shows the label. That list is the release, not a nice-to-have after the desktop review.

Submit a test quote from the phone and read what the desk receives. If the mode, the ready date, or the weight is missing because the mobile form dropped a field the desktop form has, fix the form before you celebrate the layout. Two forms are two products. The operator will use the one in their hand.

Retest when you add a banner. Banners are how first screens decay. A hiring notice, a storm notice, or a new terminal can be real news and still steal the only screen that had the move on it. Put the news where a regular will see it, and leave the first screen pointed at the freight.

The tap has to open a path that says what happens next, how fast, and what to have ready. That path is [a contact path for a logistics company](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-logistics-company).

If you want to pressure-test the first phone screen before you build the wide layout, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).
